The Purpose of Space Apps
Although Space Apps 2026 will have winners - it is important for us all to
remember that...
Space Apps, first and foremost, is about collaboration, cooperation, and
learning, not competition! We place high value on the experience gained and
the opportunities that participants have to learn and grow, We have an
incredible global community of problem solvers, and we want to celebrate the
efforts of that entire community at all levels.
All participants who are on a team that submit a project on the website by the
deadline will receive a certificate of participation in their profile!
If you do not have any Global Finalists or Winners from your Local Event, it is by
no measure a reflection on your leadership! The judging process is extremely
competitive. Only 10 teams will be recognized as Global Winners out of
thousands of submissions.
Global Winners will receive additional certificates and an invitation to a virtual Winners Celebration.

Best Use of Storytelling: The project that most creatively communicates the potential of open data
through the art of storytelling.
Global Connection: The project that best connects people around the world through technology.
Art & Technology: The project that most effectively combines technical and creative skills.
Local Impact: The project that demonstrates the greatest potential for making a difference in their
local community.

NASA Space Apps Values
At NASA Space Apps, there's always space for one more.
We strive to ensure that NASA Space Apps is a place where everyone feels they belong, where all are comfortable
being authentic, and where all are empowered to contribute to their fullest.
NASA Space Apps is committed to providing a professional and productive forum for the robust exchange of ideas.
All ideas are welcome, and we encourage our community to share them.
At all times, participants are expected to maintain professional decorum and treat one another with respect and
dignity. We value collaboration and positive problem solving.
We are a community that embraces growth, inclusivity, and mutual respect.
Bullying, discrimination, or harassment on any basis will not be tolerated.

Start with the user and the decision
In one sentence, say who faces the problem, what decision they need to make and what
your project helps them do. Name the challenge early.
Show how the data changes the result
Name the dataset and show the path from input to output. For a mapping project, show
the source layer, your processing step and the resulting decision or map. Note the date
range, resolution and key limits where relevant.
Demo one complete workflow
Walk through one realistic use case from input to result. Save an offline PDF and a
screenshot or short screen recording so the judges can see the result if the connection
Give judges something they can evaluate
Show one test, a comparison with a baseline or a worked example. Identify what you built
during the event, what the prototype can demonstrate and what still needs testing.
Rehearse the pitch and Q&A
Use the time slot announced by the organizers. Practice the handoff between speakers.
Prepare short answers on data choice, accuracy, usability and what would be needed to
deploy the project.
If you make a short video
Open with the problem, spend most of the clip on the workflow, and finish with the result.
Use readable captions and check that the public link opens on a device outside your
team. Follow the current platform limits.

Using the Gallery.
Venue rules apply from 08:00 on 14 November to 18:00 on 15 November.
Food and drinks
Eat and drink in the designated area agreed with Gallery Management. Avoid
strong-smelling, crumbly or greasy food. Cooking is prohibited. Clear away food and drinks
after use.
Waste sorting
Use indoor bins for paper and ordinary dry waste. Use outdoor bins for food waste, cups,
bottles containing liquid, food packaging and other wet waste. Keep leftovers, liquids and
odorous waste out of indoor bins.
Restrooms
Use the designated restrooms and leave them clean. Keep rubbish, paper towels, personal
items and unsuitable waste out of toilets. Keep floors dry and fixtures in place. Report
clogs, leaks or damage to Gallery Management promptly.
Overnight conduct
Keep noise low and use the agreed rest area. Leave function rooms, technical areas and
venue equipment undisturbed. Smoking, open flames, cooking and flammable or explosive
items are prohibited. Follow staff instructions for lights, electrical devices and air
conditioning. Leave building electrical, technical and fire safety systems to authorized staff.
Organizer responsibilities and venue handover
Brief all staff, contractors and attendees. Assign staff to monitor cleanliness, security and
order. Keep waste in the designated collection area and clear it before overnight. Register
overnight attendees, staff the venue overnight and coordinate access and incident
response with Gallery Management.
At 18:00 on Sunday, 15 November, the Organizing Team is responsible for waste removal,
full cleaning, restoring equipment and returning the space in its original condition for
inspection and handover.

How projects are scored.
Five criteria, up to 5 points each / Final score out of 20
Judges score each criterion from O to 5. Add the five scores (maximum 25), then multiply by 0.8 for
the final score out of 20. For example, 20 out of 25 becomes 16 out of 20.
O Impact
How important is the problem, who benefits, and how much could their situation improve? Consider
the number of people or systems reached and the depth of the benefit.
Evidence to show. Define the intended users, describe the expected change, and name a measurable
outcome or realistic way to track it.
+ Creativity
What is original in the concept, use of data, design or execution? An improvement to an existing idea
can score well if the difference is meaningful.
Evidence to show. Name the closest existing approach and show what you changed, how it works and
why it matters.
Is the method scientifically sound, technically feasible and practical for its intended users? Consider
usability, accessibility, assumptions and limitations.
Evidence to show. Show a working demo, test or calculation. Explain what you validated and what still
needs to be tested.
9 Relevance
Does the project directly address the chosen challenge and its objectives? Assess how NASA data
informs a core part of the solution.
Evidence to show. Name the challenge and datasets, then trace an input through the method to a
decision, feature or result.
Presentation
Can the audience follow the challenge, proposed solution, method and significance? Consider
structure, delivery, demo clarity and how well the story supports the evidence.
Evidence to show. Make the problem and outcome clear early. Use legible visuals and connect the demo
back to the challenge.

JUDGING CRITERIA
Impact: What is the project's potential for significant impact in both quality and quantity? Does it address a major problem or a minor one? To
what extent does it inspire or help others?
Creativity: How well does the project demonstrate originality and innovation in its approach? Does it introduce a novel concept that has not been
attempted before, or present an improvement upon existing ideas in a meaningful way? To what extent does the level of creativity distinguish it
from conventional methods, showcasing a fresh perspective or inventive execution?
Validity: Does this project present a method that is grounded in scientific principles? Does it demonstrate technical feasibility? How effectively
would it achieve its intended purpose in real-world applications? How usable or user-friendly is the project? To what extent does this influence its
practicality and accessibility?
Relevance: Does this project fully and directly address the challenge for which it was submitted, demonstrating a strong alignment with the
intended objectives? How meaningfully does it integrate NASA data, utilizing it as a core component of the proposed method rather than a
superficial addition? The depth of engagement with the data enhances the project's credibility and effectiveness.
Presentation: How effectively did the team communicate their project? How clearly did they convey the challenge, their proposed method, and
its significance? How engaging and well-structured was the storytelling? How did the clarity, organization, and delivery of their presentation play
a role in making their ideas compelling and accessible, ensuring the audience understood the project's purpose and impact?
